Tests cover the main modes and the realistic grid rule, but not unknown state names.

sections.name: File setup, ViewStyle
sections.title: Imports and view style names
sections.what: Brings in the component state type from the timeline and declares the two view names, engineering and realistic.
sections.why: A fixed list of view names means a typing mistake in a view name is caught.
sections.watch_out: Adding a third view means updating this type and the palette table below, or the code will not compile.

sections.name: RevealStyle
sections.title: Shape of a reveal result
sections.what: Defines what a reveal result contains: one mode (hidden, blueprint, ghost or solid) and one opacity number.
sections.why: Gives every caller the same two answers, so drawing code stays simple.
sections.watch_out: The opacity is used directly for drawing, so values outside 0 to 1 would look wrong.

sections.name: REVEAL_LEGEND
sections.title: Legend wording for each mode
sections.what: Holds the short text shown to the user for each visible mode. The ghost text states that opacity follows date progress, not physical progress.
sections.why: Keeps the on-screen explanation in one place, so it matches the rule.
sections.watch_out: If the rule changes without this text changing, the user is misled about what a shade means.

sections.name: revealStyle
sections.title: Decision rule for drawing a component
sections.what: Given one component's state and whether future work is shown, returns how to draw it. Unavailable is hidden. Future is a blueprint or hidden. Active is a ghost, with progress clamped to 0 to 1 and opacity from 0.3 up to 0.85. Anything else is solid.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeping the date rule here means every view draws components the same way.
sections.watch_out: A misspelled state name falls through to solid, so it looks finished.

sections.name: StylePalette
sections.title: Shape of a view palette
sections.what: Describes the settings one view needs: background and ground colours, ground transparency, blueprint line colour, whether to show a grid, whether to use environment lighting, and overall exposure.
sections.why: Groups every visual setting per view, so switching views changes them together.
sections.watch_out: Colours are stored as hex numbers, so new colours must use the same format.

sections.name: VIEW_STYLES
sections.title: Actual palette values for each view
sections.what: Engineering view uses a mid-grey drafting background with a visible grid. Realistic view uses a pale blue background, a neutral earth-toned ground with no grid, and slightly lower exposure.
sections.why: The comments say the grey backdrop keeps steel and conductors readable, and that the realistic ground is a plain plane, never a survey terrain.
sections.watch_out: The realistic view must keep the grid off and must never show terrain. Changing these values can break that promise.

summary: Decides how each component is drawn at the current point on the timeline, and holds the colour and display settings for the two view styles.
purpose: Turns a component's own dates and state into one of four drawing modes, and supplies the engineering and realistic visual themes.
why: Likely reason: keeping the date rule in one small file makes it testable and the same in every view. The header comment says the rule uses only each component's own dates.
how: First the component's state is checked. Unavailable work is hidden. Future work is a blueprint when future work is shown, otherwise hidden. Active work is a ghost whose opacity rises from 0.3 toward 0.85 with date progress. Any other state is solid. Separately, the palette table holds background, ground, line and lighting settings for each view.
inputs: A component's state and progress value from the timeline, a yes or no for showing future work, and the chosen view name.
outputs: A reveal result with a mode and an opacity number, short legend text for each visible mode, and palette settings for each view.
risks: A state name the code does not recognise is drawn as solid, so a data error looks like finished work. Palette changes affect the whole scene at once.
debug: If work looks finished too early, check the state values coming from the timeline and the progress number. If a view looks wrong, check the palette table. Run the reveal test file to see which rule broke.
